extracted.intended_audience: engineers, historians of technology, and general readers interested in early locomotive and mine-safety invention
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory historical/technical guidance on designing early locomotives and miners' safety-lamps, including engineering principles, experimental validation, and practical construction constraints from George Stephenson's work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhesion by engine weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhesion between wheel and rail can be sufficient by the mere weight of the engine to propel loaded wagons on smooth rails, making rack-rails and toothed wheels unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate by experiment (e.g., weighted frame with windlasses or having workmen ride on wagon wheels) to determine proportion of tractive power to weight; if adhesion is sufficient, avoid complex rack/leg/chain mechanisms. Example: experiments at Wylam showed smooth wheels on smooth rails could propel loads without slipping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical validation of traction and load performance
rubrics_metrics.description: A locomotive's success should be demonstrated by measured pulling capacity, speed, and performance on representative gradients and loads.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform practical trials (record loads, gradients, speeds). Example: Stephenson's first engine drew eight loaded carriages (30 tons each? aggregate noted) at about four miles per hour on a 1 in 450 gradient. Use such measurements to compare with horse haulage and judge economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy compared to horse power
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary test of a locomotive is its economy relative to horse haulage (cost of steam power vs keeping horses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calculate operational costs (fuel/coal, maintenance) and compare to horse-keeping costs; consider heating surface and steam generation capacity as key drivers of economy. Early engines were initially barely economical until improvements (steam-blast, larger heating surfaces) increased performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase heating surface to improve steam generation
rubrics_metrics.description: A larger heating surface in the boiler increases the capacity to generate steam, yielding greater effective power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design boilers (e.g., multi-tubular or returned-flue designs) to maximize heating surface without excess weight. Example: replacing single internal flue with multi-tubular arrangements later greatly improved steam production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of steam-blast to increase draft and power
rubrics_metrics.description: Conveying exhaust (eduction) steam into the chimney produces a blast that markedly increases draft, intensifies combustion, and thus more than doubles engine power without increasing weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate a pipe from the cylinder exhaust into the chimney to accelerate flue gases; this permits higher sustained speeds and enables benefits of multi-tubular boilers. Consider noise/public nuisance effects and provide mitigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noise abatement of exhaust steam
rubrics_metrics.description: High-pressure jets of exhaust steam cause noise and can be a public nuisance when locomotives run on public highways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigate by providing a reservoir immediately behind the chimney to receive waste steam after it leaves the cylinder, allowing gradual release into atmosphere to reduce noise. Balance noise control with preserving blast effect for draft if used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and directness in power transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: An economical locomotive should have few parts, simple actions, and direct modes of communicating power to the driving wheels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid complicated gearing (such as spur-wheel combinations that combine cylinder powers indirectly) which produce jerks, rattling when worn, and inefficiency. Prefer direct connections (crossheads and connecting rods) from cylinders to driving wheels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexible jointing to accommodate imperfect permanent way
rubrics_metrics.description: Joints must permit relative movement so the rigid mass of the engine can operate over rails that are not always at equal levels without causing jars or undue friction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use ball-and-socket style joints at connections (e.g., top of piston-rod to cross head, ends of connecting rods to crank-pins) so cross heads remain parallel to axles despite rail irregularities. This preserves alignment and reduces wear/shock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coupling all driving wheels for joint adhesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhesion should be shared across multiple wheels by mechanical coupling so that the driving strain is not concentrated on one rail or wheel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Couple wheel pairs using rods/cranks (horizontal connecting rods) or robust coupling mechanisms so adhesion is joint and balanced. Avoid designs that put entire strain on a single rack-rail or one-sided arrangement as in some early cog systems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Robust coupling method compatible with manufacturing capabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose coupling/crank solutions that are manufacturable and maintainable given the available forging skills and tools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While internal crank axles are mechanically desirable, if local forging cannot produce sufficiently strong cranked axles, use practical substitutes (e.g., chains over indented wheels initially, then outside coupling rods) to achieve the same functional coupling without unworkable manufacturing demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provision of suspension to reduce shocks
rubrics_metrics.description: Absence of springs causes jolts and derangement of machinery; suspension is needed to mitigate effects of uneven plateways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include springs or equivalent suspension arrangements to smooth the ride and protect boiler and mechanism. Early expedients included weighted water-tender lever arrangements to distribute mass more evenly, but springs are preferable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid combining cylinder outputs via spur-gear
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining two cylinders' powers by spur-wheels (gearing) can cause alternately propelling/being propelled interactions, jerks, and noise, especially as gear teeth wear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer direct mechanical linkage of cylinder motion to wheels (direct motion) rather than gear-based combination to ensure smoother continuous drive and reduce maintenance/noise issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design safety lamp to create strong upward chimney current
rubrics_metrics.description: A miner's lamp should have a chimney arrangement that produces a strong upward current so that burnt air ascends rapidly and prevents the surrounding inflammable air from descending to the flame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the lamp with a chimney and throat that encourage upward flow; Stephenson reasoned and tested that sufficient upward velocity at the chimney mouth prevents the explosive gas from reaching the flame even when the lamp is introduced into a blower of fire-damp.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit tube diameter and ensure sufficient internal velocity to prevent flame propagation
rubrics_metrics.description: Explosive mixtures cannot pass down sufficiently small tubes unless the current velocity is above a threshold; limiting tube diameter and maintaining a required upward current prevents explosion propagation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine safe tube diameters and requisite internal velocities by experiment for the range of explosive mixtures expected. Example: Stephenson's experiments indicated that, for a 0.4-inch diameter tube, a current of about 9 inches per second prevented explosive mixtures from coming down the tube.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple small passages or wire-gauze to discharge surrounding poisonous gases and block flame
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional small tubes or fine wire-gauze can prevent flame propagation and help discharge the 'azotic' (nitrogen/after-damp) gas that extinguishes or surrounds the flame; wire-gauze can also act as a flame barrier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase the number of small tubes or include fine wire-gauze between the flame and any receiver/source of explosive mixture. Be aware that improper placement or movement can still extinguish the lamp; experiment to balance light output and safety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lamp should maintain steady combustion in foul atmospheres
rubrics_metrics.description: A safety lamp must burn steadily in the presence of inflammable gas; motion or improper air admission can cause extinguishing or dangerous behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the air admission (slides, tube arrangement) so the flame remains steady even when exposed to gas; consider adding additional tubes to admit air to the exterior of the flame to displace azotic gases that can smother it. Test lamps under representative foul-air conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental determination of safe parameters with controlled trials
rubrics_metrics.description: Design decisions should be backed by controlled experiments to determine velocities, tube diameters, and flame behavior in explosive mixtures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up reproducible experiments (e.g., mixtures in a receiver, tubes of varying diameters, measurement of current velocity with water columns or pendulums) and repeat tests to observe thresholds. Note risks: experiments may produce accidents (e.g., 'blows up'), so include safety precautions and protective barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for social/practical constraints when implementing design changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Adoption of inventions must consider public reaction, nuisance, and the equipment/skill level of local workers; these factors influence practicality and acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address nuisance (e.g., steam blasts frightening horses) and train/prepare workmen if new tools or higher skill levels are required. Secure patronage/funding (example: Lord Ravensworth financing Stephenson) and balance ideal engineering solutions with real-world manufacturability and social acceptance.
